Second-layer calls are harder, and your confidence should show it. Their defaults come from base rates too.
In 2025 defenses sent five or more rushers on only `{python} pct(RUSH["all"])` of dropbacks
(`{python} pct(RUSH["third7"])` on third-and-7 to 10), so "four rush" is the default until a pressure tell moves
you off it. Zone was the coverage on about `{python} pct(1 - MAN_ALL)` of charted dropbacks, so "zone" is the
default, except near the goal line: man rose from `{python} pct(MAN_OPEN)` of dropbacks outside the red zone to
`{python} pct(MAN_RZ)` inside it, because a short field leaves zone defenders little deep space to sink into,
and tight coverage on every receiver is the natural answer to short throws. (FTN's man share jumps around
between seasons in a way that looks like charting rather than football, so treat these as rough.[^cov]) A
second-layer call at 60–70% is a good call; anyone who claims 90% on coverages before the snap is watching a
very predictable defense or not keeping score.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden you always know one of the two calls, your own. Watching a real game you know neither, and
neither does anyone on the field: the quarterback's pre-snap read *is* this checklist, and he gets it wrong
often enough that offenses build [hot routes](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) and post-snap reads
for the times he does. So a probability isn't a hedge. It is the most accurate description of what anyone,
including the players, knows before the snap.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"My 90% call missed, so I was wrong." Not necessarily: one in ten 90% calls *should* miss. You can't judge
a single probabilistic call by its outcome, only a pile of them. That's why the log matters, and why
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) scores a season of calls rather than a play. The mistakes to
look for are patterns: 90% calls that miss one time in three (overconfidence), or a log full of 55% calls
that come true 75% of the time (you know more than you're admitting).
:::

## Film room: one drive, nine snaps

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seahawks 2025 — the NFC Championship Game"}
**The game:** Rams at Seahawks, NFC Championship Game, January 25, 2026, at Lumen Field. Seattle, the NFC's
top seed (14–3), won 31–27 and two weeks later beat New England 29–13 in Super Bowl LX.[^nfc] In 2025 Seattle's
head coach was Mike Macdonald, its offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak (whose system comes from the Shanahan
family tree; see [Shanahan's Wide Zone Tree](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd)) and its
quarterback Sam Darnold.[^staff]

**The drive:** Seattle had gone up 24–13 early in the third quarter; the Rams answered with a touchdown to make
it 24–20 with 9:45 left in the quarter. After the touchback, Seattle drove 65 yards in nine snaps and scored on
third-and-3 from the Rams' 13, a 13-yard pass to Cooper Kupp, to go up 31–20 with 4:52 left in the third.

**Why this drive:** it has a bit of everything the checklist is for: three different personnel groups, under
center and shotgun, an empty backfield, a screen against a blitz, play-action, a no-huddle snap, two third
downs and a red-zone touchdown, against a defense that played base, nickel and dime and three different
coverage labels.

**The sources:** every fact below comes from the public charting in nflverse;[^drive] the diagrams are
typical pictures of what was charted, not the film.
:::

Here is the drive as your log would record it. The calls weren't made by watching the game. They were made
by rule from the pre-snap columns only, so hindsight can't creep in: the run-or-pass call and its confidence
come from the step 1 to 5 model, fitted on the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons; the coverage and rush calls are
the 2025 base rates for that down, distance, field zone and number of defensive backs.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-log
#| fig-cap: "The drive as a prediction log: Seattle's nine snaps from its own 35 to the end zone, NFC Championship Game, third quarter. Situation, offense and defense are the pre-snap facts in the charting (L/R hash = the ball spotted on the offense's left or right hash, so the field is the other way; UC = under center; M = motion; NH = no-huddle; box = defenders in the box). The calls were made by rule from those facts alone: run or pass from the checklist model, the 'if pass' layer (coverage family, rushers) from 2025 base rates for the situation and the number of defensive backs. The 'if pass' layer is filled in on every snap, because you make it before you know whether the ball will be thrown; the last two columns score the calls, and the pass layer is scored only on dropbacks, because coverage isn't charted on runs. Source: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting, game 2025_21_LA_SEA."
COLS = [("#", 2.2), ("Situation", 10.0), ("Offense shows", 11.4), ("Defense", 6.2), ("Call", 5.4),
        ("If pass", 9.6), ("What happened", 12.2), ("R/P", 3.8), ("Pass layer", 7.0)]


def dpers(n):
    return {4: "base", 5: "nickel", 6: "dime"}.get(int(n), "?") if pd.notna(n) else "?"


def off_txt(row, sep=" · "):
    al = {"U": "UC", "S": "gun", "P": "pistol"}.get(row.qb_location, "?")
    nb = int(row.n_offense_backfield)
    backs = "empty" if nb == 0 else f"{nb} back" + ("s" if nb > 1 else "")
    extra = [w for w, f in (("motion", row.is_motion), ("no-huddle", row.is_no_huddle)) if f]
    return f"{row.pers} · {al} · {backs}" + (sep + ", ".join(extra) if extra else "")


HASH = {"L": "L hash", "R": "R hash", "M": "middle"}


def ordinal(n):
    return {1: "1st", 2: "2nd", 3: "3rd", 4: "4th"}[int(n)]


ROWS = []
for i_, row in DRV.iterrows():
    l2 = "–"
    if row.is_pass:
        l2 = ("✓" if row.cov_hit == 1 else "✗") + "  " + ("✓" if row.rush_hit == 1 else "✗")
    ROWS.append([str(i_ + 1), f"{ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}\n{row.yrdln} · {HASH[row.starting_hash]}",
                 off_txt(row, sep="\n"),
                 f"{dpers(row.dbs)}\nbox {int(row.defenders_in_box)}", f"{row.call}\n{row.conf}%",
                 f"{row.cov_call} {row.cov_conf}%\n{row.rush_call} rush {row.rush_conf}%",
                 "\n".join(textwrap.wrap(row.result, 21)), "✓" if row.hit else "✗", l2])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.75))
blank(ax)
Wt = sum(w for _, w in COLS)
nr = len(ROWS)
RH = 2.15
H = 2.4 + 1.5 + RH * nr + 1.7
ax.set_xlim(0, Wt)
ax.set_ylim(0, H)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, 0), Wt, H, fc="#fbfaf4", ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0))
ax.text(0.8, H - 0.95, "PREDICTION LOG  ·  NFC Championship, Rams at Seahawks  ·  Seattle offense, Q3",
        fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
yh = H - 2.4 - 1.5
x = 0
for name, w in COLS:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, yh), w, 1.5, fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, yh + 0.75, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    x += w
for j, vals in enumerate(ROWS):
    yy = yh - (j + 1) * RH
    x = 0
    for (name, w), v in zip(COLS, vals):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, yy), w, RH, fc="white", ec=style.GRID, lw=0.6))
        col = style.INK
        if name in ("R/P", "Pass layer"):
            col = style.THIRD if v.startswith("✓") else (style.DEFENSE_DARK if v.startswith("✗") else style.INK_2)
        left = name in ("Situation", "Offense shows", "Defense", "If pass", "What happened")
        ax.text(x + 0.45 if left else x + w / 2, yy + RH / 2, v, ha="left" if left else "center", va="center",
                fontsize=5.9, color=col, linespacing=1.15,
                fontweight="bold" if name in ("R/P", "Pass layer", "#", "Call") else "normal")
        x += w
ax.text(0.8, 0.85, f"Run/pass: {N_HIT} of {nr} right.   Pass layer on the {int(DRV.is_pass.sum())} dropbacks: "
        f"coverage {N_COV} of {int(DRV.is_pass.sum())}, rushers {N_RUSH} of {int(DRV.is_pass.sum())}.",
        fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK, va="center")
plt.show()
```

The same drive in pictures, one pre-snap look per snap:

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-board
#| fig-cap: "The drive in pictures: a typical pre-snap look for each of the nine snaps, built from what was charted (offensive personnel, quarterback alignment, number of backs, defensive personnel, box count and the hash, all exact), with the ball on the right yard line and hash and the yellow line to gain. The players in the backfield are drawn dark and lettered (Q quarterback, R running back, F a fullback or a tight end lined up as an H-back), because one back or two is the formation clue on most of these snaps. Everything else is illustrative: the charting doesn't record exact alignments, and for runs the safeties are drawn two-high because the coverage isn't charted on runs; for passes the shell matches the charted coverage family. In the red zone (snaps 7 to 9) the secondary is drawn closer to the line, because the end zone is behind it. The ringed player is the ball carrier or the receiver the ball went to. Offense: blue circles; defense: orange squares."
SNAP_LOOK = {1: ("12_1", 5, 2, "two"), 2: ("12_2", 5, 1, "two"), 3: ("11_1", 4, 1, "two"), 4: ("13_2", 5, 2, "two"),
             5: ("11_0", 4, 2, "one"), 6: ("11_1", 4, 2, "one"), 7: ("12_2", 5, 2, "one"), 8: ("12_1", 5, 2, "one"),
             9: ("11_1L", 4, 2, "two")}
SNAP_RING = {1: "RB", 2: "RB", 3: "H", 4: "RB", 5: "RB", 6: "H", 7: "FB", 8: "X", 9: "H"}


def look_offense(kind):
    if kind == "12_1":
        return offense("ace")
    if kind == "12_2":       # a tight end as an offset H-back (two backs in the backfield)
        return [p_.moved(w=-1.5, pos="TE") if p_.key == "FB" else p_ for p_ in offense("offset_i")]
    if kind == "13_2":       # three tight ends: two in line, one as an H-back; one receiver
        o = [p_ for p_ in offense("ace") if p_.key != "X"]
        return o + [Player("FB", "TE", "off", -4.5, 1.5, label="F")]
    if kind == "11_1":
        return offense("gun_2x2")
    if kind == "11_1L":
        return offense("gun_2x2", strength="left")
    if kind == "11_0":
        return offense("gun_empty")
    raise KeyError(kind)


def look_defense(off, line, lbs, shell, dbs, rz=False):
    LINE = {4: [-5.8, -2.2, 1.0, 5.8], 5: [-6.2, -2.6, 0.0, 2.6, 6.2]}
    LB = {1: [0.8], 2: [-2.4, 2.4]}
    out = [Player(f"DL{k}", "DT", "def", 1.0, w) for k, w in enumerate(LINE[line])]
    out += [Player(f"LB{k}", "LB", "def", 4.5, w) for k, w in enumerate(LB[lbs])]
    rec = [p_ for p_ in off if p_.pos in ("WR", "TE", "RB") and abs(p_.w) > 6.0]
    left = sorted([p_ for p_ in rec if p_.w < 0], key=lambda p_: p_.w)
    right = sorted([p_ for p_ in rec if p_.w > 0], key=lambda p_: -p_.w)
    cb_d, s_d, ss_d = (5.5, 9.5, 7.5) if rz else (7.0, 12.5, 9.0)     # a short field compresses the secondary
    out += [Player("CBL", "CB", "def", cb_d, (left[0].w if left else -11.0) - 0.8),
            Player("CBR", "CB", "def", cb_d, (right[0].w if right else 11.0) + 0.8)]
    slots = left[1:] + right[1:]
    for k in range(dbs - 4):
        w = slots[k].w + (0.6 if slots[k].w < 0 else -0.6) if k < len(slots) else (-7.5, 7.5)[k % 2]
        out.append(Player(f"NB{k}", "NB", "def", 5.5, w))
    if shell == "two":
        out += [Player("FS", "FS", "def", s_d, -8.5), Player("SS", "SS", "def", s_d, 8.5)]
    else:
        out += [Player("FS", "FS", "def", s_d + 0.5, 0.0), Player("SS", "SS", "def", ss_d, 8.5)]
    return out


BALL_Y = {"L": "left", "R": "right", "M": "middle"}


fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(6.5, 5.6))
for k, ax in enumerate(axes.flat, start=1):
    row = D.loc[k]
    kind, line, lbs, shell = SNAP_LOOK[k]
    o = [p_.moved(label="") for p_ in look_offense(kind)]
    o = [p_.moved(w=2.4 * np.sign(p_.w)) if p_.key == "RB" and p_.d == -5.0 else p_ for p_ in o]   # gun: R beside Q
    dfn = [p_.moved(label="") for p_ in look_defense(o, line, lbs, shell, int(row.dbs), rz=row.yardline_100 <= 20)]
    los = 110 - row.yardline_100
    pk = Play(o, dfn, los=los, to_go=int(row.ydstogo), ball_y=BALL_Y[row.starting_hash])
    pk.highlight(SNAP_RING[k])
    fld = pk.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 15.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for p_ in o:                                     # the backfield, drawn so it reads at print size
        if p_.d < -1.6:
            bx_, by_ = fld.xy(*pk.to_abs(p_.d, p_.w))
            ax.add_patch(Circle((float(bx_), float(by_)), 0.95, fc=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9))
            lab = {"QB": "Q", "RB": "R"}.get(p_.pos, "F")
            ax.text(float(bx_), float(by_), lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.4, color="white",
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    ax.set_title(f"{k} · {ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}, {row.yrdln}, {HASH[row.starting_hash]}",
                 fontsize=7.6, loc="left",
                 color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", pad=2)
    short = off_txt(row).replace("motion", "M").replace("no-huddle", "NH")
    ax.text(0.0, -0.03, short + f"  vs  {dpers(row.dbs)}, box {int(row.defenders_in_box)}",
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=5.9, color=style.INK_2)
    ok = row.hit
    ax.text(0.0, -0.13, f"call {row.call.lower()} {row.conf}%  →  {row.result}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="left", va="top", fontsize=5.9, color=style.THIRD if ok else style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.965, bottom=0.07, hspace=0.5, wspace=0.06)
plt.show()
```

And here is how each run-or-pass call was built, step by step, the way the confidence should move in your head:

```{python}
#| label: fig-drive-trace
#| fig-cap: "How the run-or-pass confidence moved through the checklist on each snap of the drive. Each row is one snap, and each marker adds one step: the hollow circle is the probability of a pass from the situation alone, the small square adds personnel, the triangle adds the formation (quarterback alignment and number of backs), the diamond adds motion and tempo, and the large filled circle adds the box count and is the final pre-snap call. The right-hand label is what happened, ticked or crossed against the call. The biggest moves come at the triangle, the formation step: snap 5 (an empty backfield) jumps toward pass and snaps 2, 4 and 7 (two backs under center) drop toward run. The misses are the second-and-1 screen (a coin flip that landed the other way) and snaps 7 and 8, passes from under center with two tight ends, exactly the look offenses use to break the tendency. Model fitted on the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons; source: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.75))
n = len(DRV)
ys = np.arange(n)[::-1]
MARK = [dict(marker="o", s=36, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, label="situation only"),
        dict(marker="s", s=16, color=style.INK_2, label="+ personnel"),
        dict(marker="^", s=42, color=style.THIRD, label="+ formation"),
        dict(marker="D", s=16, color=style.INK_2, label="+ motion, tempo"),
        dict(marker="o", s=52, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="+ box: the final call")]
ax.axvline(0.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(0.5, n - 0.35, "coin flip", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
for y_, (i_, row) in zip(ys, DRV.iterrows()):
    pts = [row[f"p{k}"] for k in range(len(TRACE))]
    ax.plot(pts, [y_] * len(pts), color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    for k, (v, mk) in enumerate(zip(pts, MARK)):
        kw = {kk: vv for kk, vv in mk.items() if kk != "label"}
        ax.scatter([v], [y_], zorder=3 + k, **kw)
    ax.text(-0.02, y_, f"{i_ + 1}  {ordinal(row.down)} & {int(row.ydstogo)}, {row.yrdln}", ha="right", va="center",
            fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
    ok = row.hit
    ax.text(1.02, y_, ("✓ " if ok else "✗ ") + ("pass" if row.is_pass else "run") + f": {row.result}",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, color=style.THIRD if ok else style.DEFENSE_DARK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.1)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("chance of a pass, as the checklist goes on", fontsize=7.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
handles = []
for mk in MARK:
    face = mk.get("facecolor", mk.get("color"))
    edge = mk.get("edgecolor", mk.get("color"))
    handles.append(Line2D([], [], marker=mk["marker"], ls="", mfc=face, mec=edge, ms=np.sqrt(mk["s"]) * 0.95,
                          label=mk["label"]))
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.17), ncol=5, fontsize=6.4, frameon=False,
          handletextpad=0.3, columnspacing=1.0)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.24, right=0.72, bottom=0.2, top=0.95)
plt.show()
```

Now walk it the way you would live, step by step. The snap numbers match the log.

**Snap 1: first-and-10 at the Seattle 35, left hash.** 12 personnel (Kupp and Jake Bobo the receivers)
against base; under center, one back, motion: a run look, but only `{python} snap_conf(1)`, because offenses
throw from it too. George Holani runs behind the right guard for three. ✓

**Snap 2: second-and-7.** Second-and-medium leans pass, but Seattle stays in 12 personnel with a second player
in the backfield, most likely a tight end lined up as an H-back (in the backfield, just off the tackle's hip).
Two backs under center swings the call back to `{python} snap_conf(2)`. The Rams answer with a nickel, which
looks like the defense betting on a pass, until you notice *who* came on. On snap 1 the receivers were Kupp
and Bobo; now they are Kupp and Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the league's 2025 Offensive Player of the Year. On this drive
every snap with Smith-Njigba on the field drew a nickel or a dime, and every 12-personnel snap without him drew
base.[^jsn] The Rams were matching a player, not a digit: that's the "notice *which* receivers" of step 2. Kenneth
Walker loses two around the right end. The call was right; the run wasn't, and you're scoring your read, not
the offense.

**Snap 3: third-and-9 at the 36, right hash.** The run-or-pass question answers itself
(`{python} snap_conf(3)`), and everything after step 3 goes into the second layer. Seattle goes to 11 personnel
in the shotgun; the Rams go to dime (six defensive backs) with only five men in the box, a defense that wants to
keep everything in front of it and tackle short of the sticks. The base-rate calls say zone and a four-man rush,
and that's what came: four rushers, and a zone FTN labelled Cover 9, a number that means different things to
different staffs ([Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)); the figure draws
the Fangio meaning, a weak-rotation Cover 3 ([Fangio's Two-High Revolution](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)).
Darnold held the ball 2.8 seconds and found Kupp short to the left, toward the field, a throw FTN charted as a
checkdown: six yards in the air and six after the catch, a first down by three yards.

```{python}
#| label: fig-snap3
#| fig-cap: "Snap 3, third-and-9 from the right hash (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun, no motion; the Rams in dime with five in the box; four rushers; a zone labelled Cover 9; a checkdown thrown after 2.8 seconds to Cooper Kupp (H, ringed) on a short out to the left, toward the wide side of the field: six yards in the air and six after the catch for the first down. Illustrative: the alignments, the other routes, and the rotation, drawn as the weak-rotation Cover 3 meaning of 'Cover 9' (two-high before the snap, the safety away from the tight end coming down, three deep). Defensive letters: E, an end or edge rusher; T, a tackle; M, the one linebacker; $ and D, the nickel and dime backs; FS and SS, the safeties. What to notice: the quarterback's eyes (the green dashed line) start on the right, where Z's curl and Y's dig are covered by the underneath defenders sinking to the sticks, and only then does the ball go left; the conversion comes from the yards after the catch."
def snap3():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dl = [("OLB1", "OLB", 1.0, -6.6), ("DT1", "DT", 1.0, -2.0), ("DE1", "DE", 1.0, 1.2), ("OLB2", "OLB", 1.0, 6.0)]
    dfn = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w, label="T" if pos == "DT" else "E") for k, pos, d, w in dl]
    dfn += [Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 5.5, 0.6),
            Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 7.5, -15.8, label="CB"), Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.5, 15.8, label="CB"),
            Player("ND", "DB", "def", 6.0, -9.6, label="$"), Player("DM", "DB", "def", 6.0, 9.6, label="D"),
            Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.0, -8.5), Player("SS", "SS", "def", 13.0, 8.5)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=46, to_go=9, ball_y="right")
    p.highlight("H")
    p.route("X", r.go(20)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12)); p.route("Y", r.dig(12, 8))
    p.route("H", r.path((5.0, 0.0), (5.6, 3.5), (6.0, 11.0)), speed=4.6)   # a short out, run flat to the sideline
    p.route("H", r.path((6.0, 0.6)), speed=6.5)                          # ...and up the field after the catch
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -0.4)])
    p.dropback(2.5)
    protect(p)
    engage(p, ("OLB1", "DT1", "DE1", "OLB2"))
    # Cover 9 drawn as a weak rotation: the left (weak) safety comes down, the right one runs to the middle
    p.drop("FS", (9.0, -5.0), speed=5.0)
    p.drop("SS", (17.0, 0.0), speed=6.0)
    p.drop("LCB", (17.0, -16.6), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (17.0, 15.8), speed=5.5)
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 1.5)); p.drop("DM", (8.5, 11.5))
    p.drop("ND", (8.5, -12.5), speed=4.5)
    p.path("ND", [(9.0, -19.0)], speed=4.0, delay=2.8, absolute=True)   # drives on the throw
    p.read("Z")
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.8)
    return p


s3 = snap3()
animate_or_strip(s3, [0.0, 1.5, 2.85, 4.6],
                 ["Snap · dime, two-high, five in the box", "+1.5 s · three deep; QB looks right",
                  "+2.8 s · right side covered; ball goes left", "+4.6 s · twelve yards: past the sticks"],
                 lateral=(-24, 21), window=(-9.0, 19.5))
```

That's the usual shape of third-and-long: the run-or-pass call is free, the defense's plan is readable from
its personnel, and the play is decided by something you can't predict, a tackle made or missed. A second-layer
call of "zone, four rush, the ball goes short" was right, and that's as good as reading gets.

**Snap 4: first-and-10 at the 48, left hash.** Seattle goes heavy: 13 personnel (three tight ends, one
receiver), under center, two backs, motion. The Rams match with base and five linemen and edge rushers up front
(two of them listed on the roster as nose tackles), a seven-man box. The call is `{python} snap_conf(4)`, as
confident as a first-down run call gets, and that leaves time for a second layer: *which way?* Under center
there's no shotgun offset to read, so the clues are the strength (the side with more tight ends, or the
H-back's side) and the light side of the box. The charting doesn't record which side those were, so this drive
can't score a direction call. Walker went behind the right guard for eleven. In your own log, write the
direction call anyway (`l2 right, 0.6`): your eyes record what the charting doesn't.

**Snap 5: first-and-10 at the Rams' 41.** The reverse picture: 11 personnel, shotgun, and **nobody in the
backfield**. An empty backfield is the strongest pass tell in the catalogue (`{python} pct(RATE["empty"])` of
2025 empty-backfield snaps were dropbacks), and the call is `{python} snap_conf(5)`. The second layer is the
interesting part. Empty leaves only five blockers, so a sixth rusher is unblockable and the quarterback has to
beat him with a quick throw; that's why empty is so often a quick-throw formation. The Rams rushed four and
played Cover 3, and Darnold checked the ball down to Holani, who had lined up outside the backfield as a
receiver, on a shallow cross for nine.

**Snap 6: second-and-1 at the 32, right hash.** The most interesting snap of the drive. Second-and-short is
the down where offenses take chances, because even a failed play leaves a manageable third down; from the
shotgun with 11 personnel it was a pass `{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11"])` of the time in 2025. The model
says `{python} snap_conf(6)`. Why the disagreement? The model adds the down and the formation as separate
pushes and never learns that this particular pairing, the shotgun on second-and-short, throws more than the two
pushes suggest: at the formation step it says `{python} pct(D.loc[6, "p2"])` where the raw rate is
`{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11"])`. Narrow the raw rate to this exact look (one back, motion, six in the box)
and it falls to `{python} pct(RATE["look6"])`, though on only `{python} N_LOOK6` snaps. Either way it's close to
a coin flip, and there's a general lesson: when you know the base rate for the exact look, trust it over a sum of
clues. The second layer said zone (`{python} int(D.loc[6, "cov_conf"])`%) and a four-man rush
(`{python} int(D.loc[6, "rush_conf"])`%). The Rams played zone but sent five, and Darnold got the ball out in 0.7
seconds on a screen to Smith-Njigba, who caught it four yards *behind* the line, toward the field, and ran
sixteen yards after the catch. ✗ on run or pass, and a 55% call is allowed to miss: that is what 55% means.

```{python}
#| label: fig-snap6
#| fig-cap: "Snap 6, second-and-1 from the right hash (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun with motion; the Rams in nickel with six in the box; five rushers (one of them a blitzer) and Cover 3 behind them; a screen to Jaxon Smith-Njigba (H, ringed) on the left, toward the field, thrown 0.7 seconds after the snap, caught four yards behind the line, sixteen yards after the catch, tackled by an inside linebacker. Illustrative: who motioned (here the tight end, Y, across to the left), which defender blitzed (here the Will linebacker, W), and the blocks. What to notice: the third panel, when the ball is already out and the blitzer has only reached the line; with him gone, the screen side has three Seattle players (X and Y blocking, H with the ball) against two Rams defenders, the corner and the nickel."
def snap6():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = [Player("WDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, -5.8), Player("WDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -2.0),
           Player("SDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, 1.0), Player("SDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 5.8),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.5, 1.8), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 4.5, -2.2),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 5.0, -9.6), Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, -15.8, label="CB"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, 15.8, label="CB"), Player("FS", "FS", "def", 13.5, 0.0),
           Player("SS", "SS", "def", 8.5, 9.6)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=78, to_go=1, ball_y="right")
    p.highlight("H")
    p.motion("Y", to=(-1.5, -5.6), speed=5.0)                # tight end across: three to the left
    p.motion("SS", to=(8.0, 2.0), speed=3.0)                 # the safety bumps over: a zone answer
    # defense: five rush, Cover 3 behind
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("WILL", pts=[(-3.5, 0.6), (-7.1, -2.8)], speed=5.0)  # at the line when the ball comes out, then wide
    p.drop("FS", (14.0, -2.0), speed=3.0)
    p.path("FS", [(15.0, -16.0)], speed=6.0, delay=0.5, absolute=True)
    p.path("LCB", [(3.6, -14.0)], speed=3.0, delay=0.3, absolute=True)   # comes up and meets X's block
    p.drop("RCB", (13.0, 15.0), speed=5.0)
    p.path("NB", [(1.5, -11.6)], speed=4.5, absolute=True)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 0.0))
    p.path("MIKE", [(10.6, -12.8)], speed=5.5, delay=0.6, absolute=True)   # the inside linebacker makes the tackle
    p.drop("SS", (8.5, -3.0), speed=4.0)
    # offense: the screen
    protect(p)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.5, 0.4)])
    p.route("H", r.path((-1.5, 1.6), (-2.5, 3.6)), speed=4.0)
    p.route("H", r.path((16.0, 2.4)), speed=7.0)
    p.block("X", pts=[(3.2, 0.9)], speed=3.0)
    p.block("Y", target="NB")
    p.route("Z", r.go(14))
    p.dropback(0.8)
    p.pass_to("H", t=0.7)
    return p


s6 = snap6()
animate_or_strip(s6, [-1.6, 0.0, 0.75, 3.0],
                 ["−1.6 s · motion: the tight end goes left", "Snap · three to the left; one safety deep",
                  "+0.7 s · ball out; the Will is still at the line", "+3.0 s · sixteen yards after the catch"],
                 lateral=(-23, 21), window=(-8.5, 18.0))
```

Why does a screen beat a blitz? Because every extra rusher is a defender who isn't covering anyone. This was a
perimeter screen, thrown at once: the blitzing Will was one fewer Ram on the outside, so the screen side had
three Seattle players against two defenders, and the ball was gone before the fifth rusher mattered. A pressure
call against a screen is the worst outcome for a defense, and it happens because the defense was guessing too:
second-and-1 from the shotgun is a coin flip for everyone. Could step 8 have warned you? The charting can't say
whether the Will showed his blitz before the snap, so the reconstruction doesn't draw a tell. If he did (a
linebacker creeping toward the line with one safety deep), your second-layer call should have moved from "four
rush" toward "five or more, ball out fast".

**Snap 7: first-and-10 at the Rams' 20.** Back to 12 personnel, under center, two backs, motion, against base
and a seven-man box. Every step says run: `{python} snap_conf(7)`. It was play-action. Darnold faked the
handoff, left the pocket and, after 4.7 seconds, found the tight end AJ Barner short on the left for seven. ✗.
This is the miss you *should* have, the tendency-breaker built to beat the reader who believes the look: an
offense from the Shanahan tree lives on making its run and play-action looks identical
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). At
`{python} int(D.loc[7, "conf"])`% the call was honest. At 95% it would have been a misread. And the model
doesn't know it's Seattle; you would. From 12 personnel under center on first down, Seattle threw
`{python} pct(RATE["first12uc_sea"])` of the time in 2025 (`{python} N_12UC_SEA` snaps), against
`{python} pct(RATE["first12uc_all"])` for the league, so a reader who copied the team's tendencies before kickoff
would have started this snap several points closer to pass.

**Snap 8: second-and-3 at the 13, no huddle.** Seattle hurried to the line in the same personnel, under center
with one back. The call is `{python} snap_conf(8)`, and it missed again: a quick throw to Jake Bobo, out 0.6
seconds after the snap and aimed at a spot `{python} AIR8`, which FTN charts as a designed throw with no progression: a perimeter extension of the run game rather than a dropback. Incomplete. The second
layer split: in this spot (second-and-short in the red zone, four defensive backs) the 2025 base rates said man
(`{python} int(D.loc[8, "cov_conf"])`%) and five or more rushers (`{python} int(D.loc[8, "rush_conf"])`%). The Rams
did send five, but played Cover 3 behind them. Two run-call misses in a row, both passes from a run look, is not
bad reading; it's a play-caller deliberately working against his own tendency in the red zone. The
between-snaps habit (card line 13) is where you'd note it, and your next call from that look should drop
toward 55%.

**Snap 9: third-and-3 at the 13, left hash.** Shotgun, 11 personnel, motion: the model says
`{python} snap_conf(9)`. Third-and-short in the red zone is one of the few spots where man coverage is about as
common as zone (the 2025 base rate for this spot was man `{python} int(D.loc[9, "cov_conf"])`%), so the coverage
call was close to a coin flip. The Rams played zone, a Cover 6 (quarters to one side, Cover 2 to the other), set
the way Cover 6 usually is: quarters to the field, on the right, where Kupp was. They rushed four and got
interior pressure, but Darnold threw on time, 2.4 seconds after the snap, to a receiver in his progression
rather than a checkdown:[^read] Kupp on a short post, caught at the 6, six more yards after the catch,
touchdown. ✓

```{python}
#| label: fig-snap9
#| fig-cap: "Snap 9, third-and-3 at the Rams' 13, from the left hash (a reconstruction, simulated in Big Data Bowl format). Charted facts: 11 personnel in the shotgun with motion; nickel, six in the box; four rushers, with interior pressure (charted: Kobie Turner, a defensive tackle, hit Darnold); Cover 6; the ball thrown inside the progression (not a checkdown) to Cooper Kupp (H, ringed) on a post from the right side, toward the field, seven yards in the air and six after the catch for the touchdown. Illustrative: the alignments, the tight end's motion (Y), the other routes, the rusher's path, and the coverage drawn as quarters on Kupp's side and Cover 2 on the other. The nickel ($) bites on Kupp's jab outside, and the quarters safety on that side widens to help on the fade outside him and comes back too late. What to notice: the third panel, the ball leaving as the tackle comes through the B gap; and that in the red zone the deep defenders are already near the goal line, so a short post that gets inside the nickel and in front of the safety has room to run."
def snap9():
    off = offense("gun_2x2", strength="left")      # X wide right, H (Kupp) right slot, Y left slot, Z wide left
    dfn = [Player("WDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, -5.8), Player("WDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, -2.0),
           Player("SDT", "DT", "def", 1.0, 1.0), Player("SDE", "DE", "def", 1.0, 5.8),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.0, 1.5), Player("WILL", "WILL", "def", 4.0, -2.5),
           Player("NB", "NB", "def", 4.5, 7.4), Player("LCB", "CB", "def", 5.0, -15.8, label="CB"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 6.0, 15.8, label="CB"), Player("FS", "FS", "def", 10.0, -8.0),
           Player("SS", "SS", "def", 9.5, 7.0)]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=97, to_go=3, ball_y="left")
    p.highlight("H")
    p.motion("Y", to=(-1.5, -5.4), speed=5.0)                 # short motion in to a wing
    p.motion("WILL", to=(4.0, -3.4), speed=1.5)               # a bump, not a chase: zone
    # offense
    p.route("H", r.path((4.0, 0.0)), speed=5.0)
    p.route("H", r.path((0.5, 1.2)), speed=5.0)               # a jab outside...
    p.route("H", r.path((4.0, -3.2)), speed=5.0)              # ...then the post, inside the nickel
    p.route("H", r.path((0.6, -1.2)), speed=1.0)              # finds the window in front of the safety
    p.route("H", r.path((6.5, -1.5)), speed=6.5)              # and runs it in
    p.route("X", r.fade(14)); p.route("Z", r.slant(2, 6)); p.route("Y", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, -3.2)])                          # the back helps to the left
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    p.block("RG", pts=[(-1.4, 0.5), (-2.4, 0.4)], speed=1.5)  # beaten inside
    p.dropback(2.5)
    # defense: four rush; quarters to the right, Cover 2 to the left
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("SDT", pts=[(-2.0, 0.6), (-6.0, -0.2)], speed=2.6)  # through the B gap as the ball leaves
    p.drop("RCB", (12.0, 15.0), speed=4.5)
    p.drop("SS", (12.0, 12.0), speed=3.0)                      # #2 went inside: he helps on X's fade...
    p.path("SS", [(12.2, 9.4)], speed=4.5, delay=0.6, absolute=True)   # ...and comes back too late
    p.path("NB", [(4.6, 11.6)], speed=4.0, absolute=True)      # bites on the jab
    p.path("NB", [(9.5, 6.4)], speed=5.0, delay=0.9, absolute=True)
    p.drop("LCB", (3.0, -13.5), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -8.0), speed=4.0)
    p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -5.5)); p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 1.0))
    p.pass_to("H", t=2.4)
    return p


s9 = snap9()
animate_or_strip(s9, [0.0, 1.6, 2.45, 4.6],
                 ["Snap · after the motion: nickel, six in the box", "+1.6 s · Kupp jabs outside; the nickel bites",
                  "+2.4 s · ball out as the pressure arrives", "+4.6 s · touchdown"],
                 lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 22.0))
```

Add it up. The run-or-pass calls went `{python} N_HIT` for 9. The three misses were all passes from looks
that lean run: a coin flip on second-and-1, then play-action and a quick throw from under center with two tight
ends, the looks an offense uses to spend its tendency. On the `{python} N_PASS` dropbacks the second layer went
`{python} N_COV` for `{python} N_PASS` on the coverage family and `{python} N_RUSH` for `{python} N_PASS` on the
rush count. The coverage misses both came in the red zone, where the base rate leaned man and the Rams played
zone; the rush miss was the second-and-1 blitz. That's a realistic live result for a good reader, and it says
where to look harder: in the red zone, don't trust the base rate for coverage, because that's where the motion
response and the shell earn their seconds.

Three habits from the drive are worth keeping:

- **Score the read, not the play.** Snap 2 was a correct run call on a run that lost yards; your log grades
  what you could know before the snap.
- **Expect the tendency-breaker where it is cheapest.** Play-action from a heavy look on first down, and a
  quick pass from the same look in the red zone, are the classic places an offense spends a tendency. A 65%
  call that misses there is fine; a 90% call that misses there is a lesson.
- **Notice the defense's bets.** Dime with five in the box on third-and-9, a nickel the moment Smith-Njigba
  came on, five rushers on second-and-1: each is the defense making its own prediction, and each is a
  clue to the second layer.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the same drive in real tracking data"}
The figures above are simulations in the Big Data Bowl's tracking format. Real tracking data is public only
for each year's Big Data Bowl release, and none covers the 2025 playoffs (the 2026 edition used the 2023
regular season). For a play that is in a release, the real version is one call to `gridiron.bdb.prepare()`
away; [Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
walks through it.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")     # a Big Data Bowl release, downloaded from Kaggle
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=2022091100, play_id=55)   # any game and play in that release
show_animation(one, times=[-1.0, 0.0, 1.5, 3.0])              # the same video / frame strip as above
```
:::

## Between snaps: keeping the read up to date

The best clue about the next snap is often the last twenty, and two habits keep your read current while the
broadcast does something else. **After every snap,** during the replay, write the log line (card line 12),
and don't skip the clue column: after a few games it tells you which tells are working *for you*.

**At every stoppage** (a TV timeout, the end of a quarter, a change of possession), update the picture of
this team, today:

1. **What are they doing from each look?** "Three runs from 12 personnel under center on first down" is a
   game tendency. It is more current than any season number, and play-callers know it too, so expect the
   [tendency breaker](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency-breaker) when the streak gets long: not
   because a pass is owed, but because the play-caller is watching the same tally you are.
2. **What did they just change?** A new protection against a rusher who is winning, a coverage rolled toward
   a receiver who is hurting them, a run that worked coming back with a twist
   ([In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)).
3. **What does the clock want?** The score and the time left change the base rate of step 1 (a team ahead late
   runs, a team behind throws). And when fourth down comes, make it its own prediction before the offense
   decides: go, kick or punt, with a confidence, logged in the second-layer columns (`l2 go`, `l2conf 0.6`).

### When the offense goes fast, or the camera won't show you

Against [tempo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tempo) the twenty seconds shrink to five or ten, and the full
checklist won't fit. Run the short one: **1, 3, 6, 9**. Situation (you already have it from the last snap,
plus the new down and distance), formation (the single biggest clue after the situation), shell (the single
most useful second-layer clue), and the call. Drop personnel (it usually hasn't changed; that's the point of
tempo), motion (tempo offenses use less of it), and the box and leverage counts you can't finish anyway. The
measured value of what you drop is small for run or pass; the cost is mostly in your second layer, so lower
those confidences when the offense is hurrying.

The same applies when the broadcast is still on a replay at the snap, which happens more than it should.
Call it from the situation alone, write "sit" as the clue, and move on. A 60% call from the scorebug is still
a call.

The commonest problem is milder: the snap is live, but the shot is tight, and the safeties and corners are off
the top and sides of the screen. Steps 1 to 5 still work (the formation and the box are in the picture); steps
6 and 7 don't. Write `?` in the `shell` column rather than guessing, make your second-layer call from the base
rate alone, and keep its confidence at 60% or below. Then use the replay: the end-zone and high angles usually
show the whole secondary, so fill in the shell afterwards and note that you saw it late. Coverage calls you
couldn't see live get checked after the game, on the All-22, as
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) shows.

## The log, final form

Your log has grown a column at a time since Part 1. Here is its final form, the one
[Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) will score. Keep the columns from
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) (snap, quarter, clock, down,
to-go, ball on, score) and add or tighten these:

| Column | What you write | Example |
|:-------|:------------------|:-------------|
| `pers` | Offensive personnel, two digits | `12` |
| `align` | QB alignment and number of backs | `U1` (under center, one back), `S0` (empty) |
| `motion` | Motion or shift before the snap | `M` or blank |
| `box` | Defenders in the box, if you counted | `7` |
| `shell` | One-high or two-high, pre-snap; `?` if it was off screen | `1`, `2` or `?` |
| `call` | Run or pass | `R` |
| `conf` | Your stated confidence, as a decimal | `0.65` |
| `clue` | The one thing that decided it | `align` |
| `l2` | Your second-layer call (on fourth down: go, kick or punt) | `zone`, `5+`, `left`, `go` |
| `l2conf` | Its confidence | `0.6` |
| `result`, `l2result` | What happened, filled in after the snap | `P`, `zone` |

At halftime, a few lines of pandas tell you how the half went. Here it is run on the drive above, typed into
a CSV file called `nfc_title_q3.csv` with these nine lines (copy them if you want to run it yourself):

```{python}
#| echo: false
_log = pd.DataFrame({
    "snap": range(1, len(DRV) + 1), "down": DRV.down.astype(int), "togo": DRV.ydstogo.astype(int),
    "pers": DRV.pers, "align": DRV.qb_location + DRV.n_offense_backfield.astype(int).astype(str),
    "call": DRV.call.str[0], "conf": DRV.conf / 100, "clue": ["align"] * len(DRV),
    "result": np.where(DRV.is_pass, "P", "R")})
_cwd, _tmp = os.getcwd(), tempfile.mkdtemp()
_log.to_csv(os.path.join(_tmp, "nfc_title_q3.csv"), index=False)
os.chdir(_tmp)
print(_log.to_csv(index=False).strip())
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("nfc_title_q3.csv")
log["hit"] = log["call"] == log["result"]
print(f"Right on {log.hit.sum()} of {len(log)} calls ({log.hit.mean():.0%}); average stated confidence {log.conf.mean():.0%}")
bands = pd.cut(log.conf, [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.91], right=False, labels=["50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80-90"])
print(log.groupby(bands, observed=True).hit.agg(calls="size", right="mean").round(2).to_string())
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
os.chdir(_cwd)
```

Two numbers to watch over a season, not a half: your hit rate against your average stated confidence (if
you're right 70% of the time while claiming 80%, you're overconfident), and the hit rate within each band
(your 80% calls should come true about 80% of the time). Nine snaps can't tell you either; a few hundred can,
and that is what the next chapter does with them.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the live run"}
For **one half** of one game, watching one offense (one team's play-caller, so the between-snaps tally is
about one set of habits; switch teams the next time):

- **First, a warm-up.** Before kickoff, pause a recorded game the moment an offense sets, give yourself ten
  seconds, and say steps 1 to 9 out loud. Do it on five snaps. The order should feel automatic before the clock
  is real.
- **Before every snap**, run the card in order: situation, personnel, formation, motion response, box, shell,
  leverage, pressure, call. Say the call and a confidence between 50% and 90% out loud *before* the snap.
  If the broadcast is still on a replay, call it from the situation and write "sit".
- **On the snaps where you have time**, add one second-layer call with its own confidence: on likely passes,
  the coverage family or the rush (four, or five or more); on likely runs, the direction.
- **During the replay**, write the line: down, to-go, pers, align, call, conf, clue, and the second-layer
  call if you made one. Fill in the result.
- **At each stoppage**, update the tally of what this team does from each look today, and note anything it
  changed.
- **When the offense goes no-huddle**, switch to the short checklist (1, 3, 6, 9) and lower your second-layer
  confidences.
- **At halftime**, score it: hit rate, average confidence, and the hit rate of your 80%-plus calls. Keep the
  sheet. [Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) adds a second half of work to it: the All-22, the
  chart, and the score.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: first down, two backs"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-iform
#| fig-cap: "First quarter, 0–0. First-and-10 at the offense's own 30. The offense has 21 personnel (two backs, one tight end) in an I-formation: quarterback under center, fullback (F) and tailback (T) stacked behind him, the tight end (Y) on the right. The defense is in base with the strong safety (ringed) walked down to the edge of the box: eight defenders in the box, one safety deep in the middle."
off = offense("i_form")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
dfn = [p_.moved(d=6.5, w=7.4) if p_.key == "SS" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pd1 = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
pd1.highlight("SS")
fld = pd1.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-9.5, 17.0), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pd1, ["Q1  12:40", "0 – 0", "1st & 10, own 30"], at=(-7.2, -19.6))
tag(fld, pd1, "8 in the box", (8.8, 4.0), fs=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass, how sure are you? And a second layer: if it's a run, which way; if it's a pass, what kind?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Run, about 70%; if it's a run, lean left, away from the walked-down safety (55%); if it's a pass, expect play-action.** *Situation:* first-and-10 is a coin flip
(`{python} pct(RATE["first10"])` passes in 2025). *Personnel and formation:* 21 personnel with the quarterback
under center moves it a long way: on first-and-10 from that look, offenses threw only
`{python} pct(RATE["first21uc"])` of the time in 2025. *Box:* eight in the box with one safety deep is the
defense loading up against the run, and offenses facing it from this look threw a little *less* often
(`{python} pct(RATE["first21uc8"])`, though that's only `{python} N_FIRST21UC8` snaps).

So why not 85 or 90? Because this is the exact picture play-action is built for. One deep safety and eight
defenders committed to the run leave the deep middle and the space behind the linebackers thin, and an offense
that gets the linebackers to step up for the fake can throw a post or a deep crossing route behind them
([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). *Which way, if it's a run?* The I-formation hides the direction (with the fullback straight behind the
quarterback there's no offset to read), so the clue is the box. The safety who walked down did it on the tight
end's side, the formation's strength, and he is the eighth man; an offense that sees him usually runs away from
him or checks to a pass. Lean left, to the weak side, but only about 55%: plenty of teams run at the strength
anyway, with the tight end and fullback as extra blockers. A good log line: *call R, conf 0.70, clue box, l2
"left", 0.55 (if pass, PA shot)*.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the mugs on third down"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-mugs
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6 at the opponent's 42, second quarter. Shotgun, 11 personnel, two receivers each side, the back to the quarterback's left. The defense shows a pressure look: both inside linebackers (ringed) have walked up into the A gaps, either side of the center, so six defenders are at the line. Behind them, two safeties stand 12 yards deep and both corners are seven yards off."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
DM2 = {"MIKE": (1.0, 0.9), "WILL": (1.0, -0.9), "FS": (12.0, -9.0), "SS": (12.0, 9.0), "LCB": (7.0, -16.0),
       "RCB": (7.0, 16.0), "WDE": (1.0, -6.6), "WDT": (1.0, -2.6), "SDT": (1.0, 2.6), "SDE": (1.0, 6.6)}
dfn = [p_.moved(d=DM2[p_.key][0], w=DM2[p_.key][1]) if p_.key in DM2 else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pd2 = Play(off, dfn, los=68, to_go=6)
pd2.highlight("MIKE", "WILL")
fld = pd2.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pd2, ["Q2  6:15", "HOME 10 – AWAY 7", "3rd & 6, opp 42"], at=(-6.4, -19.6))
tag(fld, pd2, "two A-gap mugs", (3.6, -4.6), fs=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**It's a pass; how many will rush, and where should the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Pass, near certain; four rushers is still the best single call (about 60%), and the ball should come out
fast.** Run or pass is the cheap part: on third-and-4 to 6 from the shotgun with 11 personnel, offenses threw
`{python} pct(RATE["third46gun11"])` of the time in 2025. Spend the rest on step 8.

*Count the deep players first.* Two safeties at 12 yards and two corners seven yards off are four defenders
who are, for now, playing coverage. That leaves seven for the rush and the underneath zones, and six of them
are standing at the line. If all six rushed, there would be one defender underneath, which almost no defense
risks with the ball at midfield. Six can come only as Cover 0, man-to-man with nobody deep, and for that both
safeties have to walk down; if they're still at 12 when the ball is snapped, six isn't coming. So the realistic
menu is: both mugs bail and the four linemen rush (a bluff, with ordinary coverage behind it); one mug comes
while a lineman drops into his spot, still four rushers but from unexpected places (a
[simulated pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-simulated-pressure), the creeper of
[Zone Blitzes](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)); or one mug comes and one drops, a
five-man pressure. On third-and-4 to 6 in 2025, defenses sent five or more on only
`{python} pct(RUSH["third46"])` of dropbacks. A pressure look moves that number up, but probably not past
half, so "four rush, 60%" is an honest call, and "five or more, 40%" is the alternative you keep in mind.

*Where the ball goes:* the offense has to protect against six, so the quarterback will likely set the
protection to the mugs and have a quick answer built in. Expect a throw in under 2.5 seconds, near the sticks,
to the side a dropping linebacker has the farthest to run to. Which side that is, you can't know before the
snap: it depends on which mug drops, and that's exactly why the quarterback's answer is a read he makes after
the snap. And if a mug drops into the throwing lane, that is the simulated pressure doing its job.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: tempo after a first down"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-tempo
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-2 at the opponent's 45, third quarter. The offense just ran for 8 yards on first down out of 11 personnel and sprinted to the line without huddling or substituting. Now it shows trips right: the tight end (Y) attached to the right tackle, a slot receiver (H) and Z outside him, with X alone on the left. The defense, which had its base personnel on the field (three linebackers, two corners, two safeties), couldn't substitute: its strongside linebacker (S, ringed) has had to walk out over H, a receiver, in space."
off = offense("gun_trips")
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
DM3 = {"SAM": (4.5, 9.2), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.2), "WILL": (4.5, -2.8), "FS": (12.5, -8.5), "SS": (12.5, 9.5),
       "LCB": (7.0, -16.0), "RCB": (7.0, 17.6)}
dfn = [p_.moved(d=DM3[p_.key][0], w=DM3[p_.key][1]) if p_.key in DM3 else p_ for p_ in dfn]
dfn = [p_.moved(label="CB") if p_.pos == "CB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]
pd3 = Play(off, dfn, los=65, to_go=2)
pd3.highlight("SAM")
fld = pd3.draw(lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
scorebug(fld, pd3, ["Q3  9:02", "HOME 17 – AWAY 17", "2nd & 2, opp 45  ·  no huddle"], at=(-6.4, -19.6))
tag(fld, pd3, "base defense, frozen", (9.0, -3.0), fs=6.8)
plt.show()
```

**What is the offense hunting, and what's your call?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A lean to pass, about 60%, aimed at the linebacker on the slot.** *Situation:* second-and-2 is a run
down overall (only `{python} pct(RATE["second12"])` passes in 2025), but from the shotgun with 11 personnel
it was `{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11"])`, and with no huddle `{python} pct(RATE["second12gun11nh"])` (a
small sample, `{python} N_SECOND12NH` snaps, so don't lean on the decimal). Second-and-short is also the down
where offenses take shots, because a failure still leaves third-and-short.

*Personnel and tempo:* this is the [substitution freeze](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-freeze)
at work. Because the offense didn't substitute, the defense had no guaranteed chance to swap a linebacker for a
nickel back, so its strongside linebacker is now standing over a slot receiver in space. That is the matchup the
offense sprinted to the line to get: a quick throw or a crossing route at the linebacker, or a deeper shot if
the safeties cheat up for the run.

*Why only 60%:* walking the Sam out leaves the frozen base defense only six in the box, and with the tight end
attached the offense has six blockers for them, a fair fight for a run. A team that just gained eight on the
ground may simply run it again. Tempo tells you the offense likes
something about this picture; it doesn't tell you which of the two things it likes. A good log line: *call P,
conf 0.60, clue tempo, l2 "target the slot", 0.55*.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Order beats speed.** The master checklist asks nine questions in the order the game answers them
  (situation, personnel, formation, motion response, box, shell, leverage, pressure, call), and each answer
  changes what the next clue means.
- **Run or pass is mostly settled by step 3.** In 2024–2025 data the situation and the formation did almost all
  the work; motion, tempo and the box added under a point. Spend the later steps on the second layer: coverage,
  rush, where the ball goes.
- **Tells are leans with reasons.** Every tell in the catalogue leaks because of physics or assignment, and
  every one is broken on purpose by somebody. Trust them in proportion to how often they're right, and expect
  the break where it's cheapest for the offense.
- **Say a number.** A stated confidence between 50% and 90%, made before the snap, turns watching into
  something you can score. Start from the base rate, move with strong clues, and rarely go past 90.
- **Score the read, not the play.** A correct call on a failed play is a correct call, and a 65% call that
  misses on a tendency-breaker is honest reading.

[^clock]: NFL Football Operations, "Football terms" glossary (the 40-second play clock, and the 25-second clock after certain administrative stoppages): https://operations.nfl.com/learn-the-game/nfl-basics/terms-glossary/

[^radio]: NFL, *Official Playing Rules*, Rule 5, Section 3, Article 3 ("Speakers in helmets"): coach-to-player communication "is cut off when the play clock reaches 15 seconds or the ball is snapped, whichever occurs first." Rulebook: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ . The rule and its history are covered in [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd).

[^gawande]: Atul Gawande, *The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right* (Metropolitan Books, 2009), on aviation checklists, the surgical safety checklist, and "do-confirm" against "read-do" checklists.

[^rates]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (quarterback alignment, tempo) and participation (personnel), 2025 regular season, runs and dropbacks with a down recorded. "Pass" is nflverse's `pass` flag, so sacks and scrambles count as passes, as in your log.

[^motion]: Daire Carragher, "NFL pre-snap motion usage reaches new highs across the NFL," PFF (Feb. 23, 2026): https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-pre-snap-motion-usage-reaches-new-highs-across-the-nfl . PFF's series counts shifts and motion together and is not comparable with FTN's `is_motion` flag, which nflverse defines as motion "before or at the time of the snap."

[^mcdaniels]: Phil Perry, "Super Bowl 60 preview: Four matchups that will decide Patriots-Seahawks," NBC Sports Boston (Feb. 8, 2026): https://www.nbcsportsboston.com/nfl/new-england-patriots/super-bowl-2026-preview-matchups-drake-maye-seahawks/766995 ("if we have the ball for 70 snaps in the game, 65 of them are gonna look the same before the ball's snapped").

[^hash]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`pass_location`, `run_location`) and FTN charting (`starting_hash`, `is_screen_pass`), 2025 regular season, plays snapped from a hash that went left or right. FTN does not say whose left and right it means; the screens are the evidence that it is the offense's, because a screen is the play most often sent to the wide side, and from FTN's "L" hash most screens go right. The same check shows that runs from a hash split almost evenly (`{python} pct(FIELD["run"])` to the field), so the hash alone doesn't call a run's direction.

[^twohigh]: NFL.com, "The coverage that turned the Seahawks into Super Bowl winners and is taking the NFL by storm" (Next Gen Stats): https://www.nfl.com/news/the-coverage-that-turned-the-seahawks-into-super-bowl-winners-and-is-taking-the-nfl-by-storm (two-high on 32.9% of dropbacks in 2018, 42.0% in 2025).

[^worth]: Course calculation: nested ridge-penalised logistic regressions (numpy) on nflverse play-by-play, FTN charting and participation, trained on 2024 regular-season runs and dropbacks and tested on all 32,813 in 2025. Each step adds its charted columns (the full list is in the chapter's code). nflverse's own `xpass` model, which uses only the situation, calls 71% of the same snaps correctly.

[^bands]: Same model and data as the chart of what each step is worth, using steps 1 to 3 only. Confidence is the model's probability for whichever side it called.

[^tetlock]: Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner, *Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction* (Crown, 2015), on the forecasting tournaments in which forecasters who used fine-grained numerical probabilities, kept score and updated often were more accurate.

[^overconf]: Sarah Lichtenstein, Baruch Fischhoff and Lawrence D. Phillips, "Calibration of probabilities: The state of the art to 1980," in Daniel Kahneman, Paul Slovic and Amos Tversky (eds.), *Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases* (Cambridge University Press, 1982), pp. 306–334: the review that established overconfidence as the usual pattern in people's probability judgments. The Brier figures are a course calculation: a call that says *c* and comes true at rate *q* scores *q*(1 − *c*)² + (1 − *q*)*c*² on average, with *q* set to the model's top-band accuracy.

[^cov]: Course calculation from nflverse participation (`defense_man_zone_type`) and FTN charting (`n_pass_rushers`), 2025 regular-season dropbacks with a rush count recorded; coverage share among those charted man or zone. On the season-to-season jumps in FTN's man share (28.8% in 2022 under the earlier NGS source, then 41.2%, 48.3% and 30.8% for 2023–2025), see the course's notes on the 2022/2023 source break in [Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).

[^nfc]: Score, date and site from nflverse schedules and play-by-play (game `2025_21_LA_SEA`: Seattle 31, Los Angeles Rams 27, January 25, 2026, Lumen Field); also "2025–26 NFL playoffs," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_NFL_playoffs . Seattle's 14–3 record and NFC top seed, and Super Bowl LX (Seattle 29, New England 13, February 8, 2026): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX .

[^staff]: Seattle's 2025 staff as listed for Super Bowl LX: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LX . Darnold and Kupp (released by the Rams) both signed with Seattle in March 2025: https://www.si.com/nfl/cooper-kupp-signs-seahawks-rams-release .

[^drive]: nflverse play-by-play, participation and FTN charting for game `2025_21_LA_SEA`, Seattle's drive beginning at 9:41 of the third quarter. The charting records personnel (including who was on the field), the quarterback's alignment, backs, motion, tempo, the hash, box count, rushers, coverage label and time to throw, but not exact alignments or the routes of receivers who weren't thrown to. Charting is done by people and contains errors; the labels are FTN's, not the teams'.

[^jsn]: Personnel and the players on the field from nflverse participation (`offense_players`, `defense_personnel`) for the drive's nine snaps, with names from nflverse rosters. Smith-Njigba's award: NFL.com, "List of NFL Honors award winners from 2025 NFL season": https://amp.nfl.com/news/list-of-nfl-honors-award-winners-from-2025-nfl-season .

[^read]: FTN's `read_thrown` field (nflverse FTN data dictionary: https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html) codes this throw as a read in the progression, not a checkdown or a designed throw; which read is ambiguous in the 2025 file, and [Film Study](15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd) shows how to check calls like this one on the All-22.
